title: Air Traffic Control Services & Communications Quiz
description: Test your knowledge of ATC services, radio communications, transponder operations, and flight plans from AIM Chapter 4

questions.question: What does CTAF stand for and what is its purpose?
options: Controlled Traffic Advisory Frequency - for ATC coordination
Common Traffic Advisory Frequency - for airport advisory practices at non-towered airports
Center Traffic Alert Frequency - for en route advisories
Control Tower Advisory Frequency - for tower communications
questions.explanation: CTAF (Common Traffic Advisory Frequency) is designated for carrying out airport advisory practices at airports without an operating control tower. It may be UNICOM, MULTICOM, FSS, or tower frequency.

questions.question: What is the standard MULTICOM frequency used when no tower, FSS, or UNICOM is available?
questions.explanation: 122.9 MHz is the MULTICOM frequency used at airports with no tower, FSS, or UNICOM. 122.75 MHz is used for air-to-air communications between private fixed-wing aircraft.

questions.question: What information is included in an ATIS broadcast?
options: Airport name, phonetic code, time, weather, instrument approach, and runway in use
questions.explanation: ATIS includes: airport/facility name, phonetic letter code, time (UTC), weather (wind, visibility, sky condition, temperature, dewpoint, altimeter), instrument approach, and runway in use.

questions.question: What should you say to indicate you have received the ATIS information?
questions.explanation: Say 'Information [Alpha/Bravo/etc.] received' to indicate you have the current ATIS. 'Have the numbers' only indicates wind, runway, and altimeter - not the full ATIS.

questions.question: What are the two types of safety alerts ATC may issue?
options: Terrain/obstruction alert and aircraft conflict alert
Mode C alert and radar contact alert
questions.explanation: ATC issues: (1) Terrain/Obstruction Alert when aircraft altitude places it in unsafe proximity to terrain/obstructions, and (2) Aircraft Conflict Alert when another aircraft creates unsafe proximity.

questions.question: What does MSAW stand for and what does it do?
options: Minimum Standard Altitude Warning - warns of low altitude in mountains
Mode Select Altitude Warning - selects safe altitudes
Minimum Safe Altitude Warning - alerts controllers to unsafe terrain proximity
Mandatory Safe Altitude Watch - monitors all aircraft altitudes
questions.explanation: MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) is an automated function that alerts controllers when a Mode C equipped aircraft is below or predicted to be below minimum safe altitude.

questions.question: What services are included in basic radar service for VFR aircraft?
options: Safety alerts, traffic advisories, limited vectoring, and sequencing where established
questions.explanation: Basic radar services for VFR include: safety alerts, traffic advisories, limited radar vectoring (workload permitting), and sequencing at locations with established procedures.

questions.question: What does the squawk code 7500 indicate?
questions.explanation: Squawk 7500 indicates hijacking/unlawful interference. Memory aid: '75 - taken alive' (hijack), '76 - need a fix' (radio failure), '77 - going to heaven' (emergency).

questions.question: What does the squawk code 7600 indicate?
questions.explanation: Squawk 7600 indicates radio/communication failure. If experiencing comm failure, squawk 7600 and continue to your destination following lost communication procedures.

questions.question: What does the squawk code 7700 indicate?
questions.explanation: Squawk 7700 indicates an emergency. This code alerts ATC and triggers special handling. Use when declaring an emergency.

questions.question: What is the standard squawk code for VFR aircraft not receiving radar services?
questions.explanation: VFR aircraft not in contact with ATC should squawk 1200. When receiving radar services, ATC will assign a discrete transponder code.

questions.question: When must you have Mode C altitude reporting capability?
options: In Class A, B, C airspace and above 10,000 MSL (except below 2,500 AGL)
questions.explanation: Mode C is required in: Class A, B, C airspace; within 30 NM of Class B primary airports (Mode C veil); and at/above 10,000 MSL except when at/below 2,500 AGL.

questions.question: What is a 'cleared as filed' clearance?
options: Clearance to fly exactly as you filed with no changes
Clearance to proceed via the route filed with possible altitude/departure changes
Clearance to file a new flight plan
questions.explanation: 'Cleared as filed' authorizes flight via the route filed. However, ATC may still assign different altitude, departure procedure, or include other restrictions.

questions.question: What is the correct readback of a clearance?
options: Full readback of route, altitude, and any hold short instructions
questions.explanation: Pilots should read back: route, altitude, hold short instructions, and any runway assignments. This confirms understanding and helps catch errors.

questions.question: What does 'radar contact' mean?
options: Your aircraft has been identified on radar and radar services are being provided
questions.explanation: 'Radar contact' means ATC has identified your aircraft on radar and will provide applicable radar services. You'll receive a discrete transponder code.

questions.question: What does 'radar service terminated' mean?
options: Radar services no longer being provided; squawk 1200 if VFR
questions.explanation: 'Radar service terminated' means ATC is no longer providing radar services. VFR aircraft should squawk 1200 and are responsible for their own navigation and traffic avoidance.

questions.question: What is the proper phraseology to request VFR flight following?
options: Request VFR advisories or request flight following
questions.explanation: Request 'VFR advisories' or 'flight following' from approach/center. Include: callsign, aircraft type, position, altitude, destination, and request.

questions.question: What should you include in an initial call to ATC?
options: Your callsign, position, altitude, and request
questions.explanation: Initial call should include: facility name, your callsign, aircraft type, position, altitude, transponder code (if assigned), destination, and request.

questions.question: What is a 'Land and Hold Short Operation' (LAHSO)?
options: Holding short of runway before takeoff
Landing and stopping before an intersecting runway/taxiway/point
questions.explanation: LAHSO requires landing and stopping before an intersecting runway, taxiway, or designated point. Pilots can decline LAHSO; acceptance is not mandatory for Part 91.

questions.question: When can a pilot decline a LAHSO clearance?
options: Anytime - pilot acceptance is voluntary for Part 91
questions.explanation: Pilots operating under Part 91 may decline LAHSO clearances. If you're unable to comply, simply state 'unable' and you'll receive alternative instructions.

questions.question: What does 'position and hold' (now 'line up and wait') mean?
options: Taxi onto the runway and wait for takeoff clearance
questions.explanation: 'Line up and wait' (formerly 'position and hold') means taxi onto the runway and await takeoff clearance. You are NOT cleared for takeoff.

questions.question: What does 'immediately' mean in ATC communications?
options: Comply without delay - safety of aircraft may be involved
questions.explanation: 'Immediately' means comply without delay. This word is used when safety of aircraft is involved or when expeditious compliance is required.

questions.question: How should you report leaving an altitude?
options: Report only at the new altitude
questions.explanation: Report altitude changes as: 'Leaving [current altitude] for [assigned altitude]'. This helps ATC maintain separation and traffic sequencing.

questions.question: What does 'say altitude' mean?
questions.explanation: 'Say altitude' is ATC requesting your current indicated altitude. Respond with your current altitude as shown on your altimeter.

questions.question: What is the correct phraseology when unable to comply with an ATC instruction?
questions.explanation: Say 'Unable' followed by the reason if possible. ATC will provide alternative instructions. Never comply with an instruction that would compromise safety.

questions.question: What are Flight Service Stations (FSS) primary services?
options: Weather briefings, flight plan processing, en route advisories, search and rescue
questions.explanation: FSSs provide: pilot briefings, flight plan processing, en route advisories, search and rescue services, assistance to lost/emergency aircraft, relay ATC clearances, broadcast weather and NOTAMs.

questions.question: What is the standard direction of turns in a traffic pattern?
options: Always left turns unless otherwise indicated
questions.explanation: Standard traffic pattern uses left turns. Right traffic patterns are designated and noted in the Chart Supplement. Always check for non-standard patterns.

questions.question: When should you obtain a special VFR clearance?
options: When weather is below basic VFR minimums but at least 1 SM visibility and clear of clouds
For all flights in Class B airspace
questions.explanation: Special VFR allows flight in controlled airspace when weather is below basic VFR but at least 1 SM visibility and clear of clouds. Requires ATC clearance.

questions.question: What is ADS-B?
questions.explanation: ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast) broadcasts aircraft position and other information from GPS. ADS-B Out is required in most controlled airspace.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the phonetic alphabet in aviation?
options: To ensure clear communication and prevent misunderstanding
questions.explanation: The phonetic alphabet (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie...) ensures clear communication, especially for callsigns and clearances, preventing potentially dangerous misunderstandings.
